To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the growth exponent of pyramids in molecular beam epitaxial growth is z=4, that there is no mechanism that can limit the growth of the structures, and that the roughness of the growing film is thus $\alpha=1$.
the slope selection of pyramidlike structures is controlled by the crystalline symmetry of the film.
the dynamic exponent of slope selection in molecular beam epitaxial growth is $z\sim4$ and the roughness exponent of the growing structure is $\alpha\ensuremath{\sim}1$.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the dynamics of growth processes.
the growth of thin films by molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) on a vicinal substrate.
the growth of surfaces under the conditions typical for molecular beam epitaxy (MBE), where the surface is exposed to a flux of atoms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the growth mode in MBE is a combination of a diffusion-controlled mechanism and an instability that leads to a selection of slope.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the growth of pyramids on a surface under MBE conditions is similar to the growth of domains in a conserved order-parameter system, and that the growth of the surface is controlled by the same dynamical exponent $z$.
we have found a simple Langevin model that describes the roughness and growth of pyramids on a surface.
we have shown that the roughening transition in molecular beam epitaxial growth is of Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) universality class.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the selection of a particular crystallographic orientation of the growing structures is the key to understanding the growth of pyramids and their coarsening.
the growth of the pyramidlike structures can be understood by a simple model that does not require the introduction of new concepts.
a simple kinetic model can be used to describe the growth of complex, self-affine structures.
